title: Reactivity Models
summary: Virtual-DOM diffing and fine-grained signal reactivity solve the same problem — knowing what changed — with opposite strategies: re-render-then-compare versus track-every-dependency. Both trade points show up constantly in framework-comparison interviews.

slides.markdown:
Every framework has to answer the same question after state changes: **which parts of the UI actually need updating?** The naive answer — re-render everything, always — would be correct but far too slow for anything beyond a toy app.

The two dominant answers you'll be asked to compare are **virtual-DOM diffing** (React's approach: re-run the whole component's render function, compare the result to last time, patch only the differences) and **fine-grained reactivity** (Vue 3's and Svelte's approach: track exactly which values a piece of UI depends on, and update only that piece directly when one of those values changes).

This isn't a trivia distinction — it's the single biggest architectural fork between mainstream frameworks, and it explains performance characteristics, mental-model complexity, and a chunk of interview questions like "why does React re-render a whole subtree by default."

React's model, in three steps, every time state changes:

1. **Render.** Re-run the component function (and every descendant that isn't memoized) to produce a new tree of lightweight JS objects describing the UI — the **virtual DOM**. This tree is cheap to build; it's plain objects, not real DOM nodes.
2. **Diff.** Compare the new virtual tree to the previous one, node by node, to figure out exactly what changed.
3. **Patch.** Apply only the minimal set of real DOM mutations needed to bring the actual page in line with the new tree.

The key insight: **real DOM operations are expensive, but building and comparing plain JS objects is cheap.** By doing the expensive comparison work in memory first, React avoids touching the real DOM for anything that didn't actually change, even though it re-ran the render function for the whole subtree to find out.

slides.sectionTitle: Fine-grained reactivity: track, then update directly
slides.subTitle: Signals
slides.markdown:
Signal-based reactivity (Vue 3's refs, Svelte 5's runes, SolidJS's signals) takes the opposite bet: instead of re-rendering a whole component to *discover* what changed, it tracks **exactly which pieces of the UI read which reactive value** at setup time, then updates only those specific DOM bindings when that value changes — no re-render, no diff, no virtual tree involved.

Mechanically: reading a signal inside a template or computation registers that location as a **subscriber**. When the signal's setter is called, it notifies its subscribers directly, and each one updates the one DOM node or attribute it's responsible for. The component function itself typically only runs **once**, at setup — not on every update the way a React component's function body does.

The trade a framework makes here: more setup machinery (proxies, dependency tracking) to get precision that skips the "figure out what changed" step entirely.

Right, labelled "Fine-grained (Signals)": State change -> Notify only the signal's registered subscribers -> Direct DOM update, no diff, no re-render >>>

slides.sectionTitle: React's re-render vs Vue/Svelte's compiled reactivity
slides.markdown:
| | React (virtual DOM) | Vue 3 / Svelte (fine-grained) |
|---|---|---|
| **On state change** | re-runs the component function, then diffs | notifies only the specific bindings that read that value |
| **What runs again** | the whole component subtree's render logic (unless memoized) | nothing extra — only the exact DOM update fires |
| **How dependencies are known** | not tracked; discovered by re-rendering and comparing | tracked automatically at setup, via proxies (Vue) or compiler analysis (Svelte) |
| **Manual opt-out needed?** | yes — `memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback` to skip unnecessary re-renders | rarely — the framework already knows the precise dependency |

Neither is strictly "better" — React's model is simpler to reason about ("the function just re-runs") at the cost of needing manual memoization for performance; fine-grained reactivity needs no manual opt-out for typical cases but relies on framework-level tracking machinery (Proxies, compile-time analysis) that's more magic under the hood.

slides.sectionTitle: Why fine-grained reactivity can skip diffing entirely
slides.markdown:
Diffing exists to answer one question: **what changed?** Virtual-DOM frameworks answer it by comparing two full trees after the fact, because they don't know in advance which parts of the UI depend on which state.

Fine-grained reactivity makes that question unnecessary by answering it **in advance, once, at setup time.** When a signal is read inside a reactive scope, that read is recorded as a subscription. So when the signal changes, the framework already has the exact list of "things that depend on this" — there's nothing left to discover by comparison, because the dependency graph was built the moment the UI was created, not rebuilt on every update.

This is the mechanical reason "no virtual DOM" is often cited as a Svelte/SolidJS selling point: it's not that virtual DOM is slow in absolute terms, it's that an entire category of work (build a tree, walk both trees, compute a diff) is structurally unnecessary once you know the dependency graph up front.

slides.sectionTitle: Mental-model simplicity vs raw update performance
slides.markdown:
The trade-off interviewers want you to name explicitly:

- **React's model is simpler to reason about.** "State changed → the function re-runs → you get a fresh description of the UI" has almost no hidden machinery. The cost shows up later, as a performance problem you have to actively manage (unnecessary re-renders), not as an upfront conceptual cost.
- **Fine-grained reactivity is more performant by default**, because it updates exactly what needs updating with no wasted re-render work — but the mental model requires trusting a dependency-tracking system you can't fully see (a Proxy intercepting property access, or a compiler rewriting your code).

Neither framework escapes this trade — Vue and Svelte occasionally surprise developers when reactivity *doesn't* track something (destructuring a reactive object often breaks tracking in Vue, for instance), which is the fine-grained model's version of React's "why did this re-render" surprise.

slides.sectionTitle: Assuming reactivity looks the same everywhere
slides.markdown:
A common mistake candidates make: assuming all frameworks either "have a virtual DOM" or "don't," as a binary. In reality there's a spectrum, and mixing up where a framework sits on it is a fast way to lose credibility.

- **React**: virtual DOM, always. Every state update re-renders the component function.
- **Vue 3**: has a virtual DOM internally, but its reactivity system (Proxy-based refs) *also* tracks fine-grained dependencies, so it can skip re-rendering whole subtrees that a signal doesn't affect — it's a hybrid, not a pure fine-grained system.
- **Svelte**: no virtual DOM. The compiler generates direct DOM-update instructions ahead of time, so there's no tree to diff at runtime at all.
- **SolidJS**: no virtual DOM, and no component re-rendering — a component function runs once, and JSX expressions compile down to fine-grained signal subscriptions, closer to Svelte's model than React's.

Saying "Vue also uses a virtual DOM" without the fine-grained-tracking caveat, or lumping Svelte and React together as "basically the same, just different syntax," both read as surface-level knowledge.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering "why does React re-render a whole subtree"
slides.markdown:
This is one of the most-asked framework-comparison questions, and a complete answer names both the mechanism and the trade-off:

1. **Mechanism**: React doesn't track which specific values a component depends on. A state update re-runs the component function unconditionally, producing a new virtual tree, and relies on diffing that tree against the previous one to find the minimal real-DOM patch.
2. **Why**: this is a deliberate simplicity choice — no dependency-tracking machinery, no proxies, no compiler magic. "Re-run and compare" is easy to reason about and debug.
3. **The cost**: re-running child component functions that didn't need to change is real, avoidable work — which is exactly why `React.memo`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback` exist, as manual opt-outs for a cost the framework doesn't avoid automatically.
4. **The contrast**: fine-grained frameworks (Vue's Proxy-based refs, Svelte's compiled reactivity) avoid this re-render step by tracking dependencies up front, trading upfront tracking machinery for automatic precision.

The next topic in this group — reconciliation — goes one level deeper into exactly how the diff step decides what counts as "the same node updated" versus "a different node entirely," which is where `key` and list-reordering bugs come from.
